meta.title: Gastaldi's Rome: a plague-response wiki
meta.edition: Girolamo Gastaldi, Tractatus de avertenda et profliganda peste politico-legalis. Bologna, 1684.
meta.coverage: Roman plague response of 1656–1657, with collected follow-up orders through 1 March 1658.
meta.countingNote: 261 chapters in the book; 204 edict/order and operational-instruction chapters (42–245). Several chapters contain multiple provisions; repeated orders, renewals and repeals are not distinct NPIs.
meta.method: Analytical English paraphrases of the checked workbook and its primary-source review. Every operational chapter is represented. This is not a diplomatic transcription or proof of uniform implementation or effectiveness.
meta.relatedNote: Related chapters share editorial themes; links do not establish historical sequence or causation.
meta.groupCountNote: Group counts use one primary filing category per chapter. Thematic filters also include cross-tags, so their totals can overlap.

groups.name: Governance, records and legal continuity
groups.measures: Health congregation and commissioners; district teams, street captains and notaries; printed orders and notices; reporting chains; hospital and property registers; inspection and finance; preservation of archives; emergency hearings, wills and pensions.
groups.analysis: Makes restrictions administratively executable. Recordkeeping, supply finance and continuity of legal business were parts of the response, not merely background.

groups.name: Surveillance and contact tracing
groups.measures: Household censuses and repeated visits; visual roll calls; illness and death notification; symptom-based triggers; nightly physician returns; tracing arrivals, companions, addresses and possessions; lodging and secondhand-goods ledgers; reporting absentees and prohibiting aliases.
groups.analysis: Links detection to case investigation and action. Independent clergy and medical reports provided overlapping channels; actual completeness of reporting is not established by the rules alone.

groups.name: Borders, travel and transport
groups.measures: Place-specific bans and cordons; controlled city gates and approved ports; health passes with identity, origin and route endorsements; cargo manifests; walls, guards, coast signals, boat and swimming restrictions; authorized mail channels; separate maritime routes and landing points.
groups.analysis: Seeks to prevent importation while allowing authorized movement. Certificates were conditional evidence, and some bans applied despite valid papers.

groups.name: Isolation, quarantine and hospital separation
groups.measures: Seal and mark affected houses; cordon Trastevere and the ghetto; separate infected, suspected, exposed and convalescent people; licensed home care followed by stricter institutional transfer; observation before ordinary-hospital admission; cohort arrivals; restrict visitors, exits and belongings; controlled release.
groups.analysis: A changing, layered separation system. Quarantine periods depended on the situation; a universal forty-day rule would misrepresent the Roman orders.

groups.name: Gatherings and everyday contact
groups.measures: Suspend nonfood markets, schools, festivals and selected tribunal business; limit tavern tables to four; restrict nighttime visits/stays at courtesans’ houses; permit only necessary sick visitors; disperse spectators around patient transfers; use barriers, distant handovers and contact-free deliveries. Marino has a separate five-person gathering limit.
groups.analysis: Reduce opportunities for contact while preserving specified essentials. Rules were place-specific and altered over time; the four-person rule was for tavern tables, not every encounter.

groups.name: Staffing, worker protection and care access
groups.measures: Retain and register physicians, surgeons and barbers; recruit and pay clinical staff, confessors and midwives; separate exposed and clean teams and housing; distinctive rods and garments; gloves, waxed clothing, tools and vinegar cloths; rounds and patient records; staff quarantine; no unauthorized fees or tips.
groups.analysis: Preserves staffing and separates occupational exposures. Some procedures resemble modern infection control in purpose; their specific protective efficacy cannot be assumed.

groups.name: Goods, premises and decontamination
groups.measures: Regulate secondhand trade and exposed goods; inspect, inventory, label, escort, wash, boil, heat, fumigate, air or selectively burn material; distinguish clean and dirty sites and teams; cleanse houses and latrines and limewash rooms; disinfect mail and packaging; secure valuables and legal papers and return property against receipts.
groups.analysis: A detailed system for treating materials believed contagious, coupled with protection of ownership. Different procedures had different likely effects; 'disinfection' here names the historical practice, not proven sterilization.

groups.name: Sanitation, animals and the dead
groups.measures: Clean streets, markets, drains, wells and courtyards; remove slaughter waste and stagnant water; regulate foul burning and silkworm waste; confine or kill roaming animals; require burial permission; use dedicated corpse teams, boats, routes and burial grounds; cover graves and avoid disturbing remains.
groups.analysis: Combines cleanliness, occupational safeguards and beliefs about unhealthy air. Some waste was directed into the Tiber; animal killing and fumigation should not be treated as modern evidence-based vector control.

groups.name: Food, fuel, agriculture and commerce
groups.measures: Maintain food markets and segregated exchanges at gates; clean supplier inns and return certificates; protect carriers from tolls, detention and nonpayment; guarantee purchasing; inventory firewood transport; regulate bread price, weight and quality and bakery rents; sustain harvests, sowing and cultivation; restrict suspect foods.
groups.analysis: Makes restrictions materially sustainable and prevents supply collapse. Some fruit, grape and mushroom bans reflected contemporary ideas of disease and the wish to avoid illness resembling plague.

groups.name: Relief and rules targeting particular populations
groups.measures: Deliver food and necessities during confinement; support poor patients and infant feeding; free designated care and disinfection; compensate certain destroyed or damaged goods; organize charitable funds; classify, license, employ or confine beggars; administer separate ghetto institutions and communal obligations; exclude Jews and Roma under some travel rules.
groups.analysis: Support and coercion coexisted. Compensation and amnesty address incentives to conceal illness or property; status-based exclusions and unequal obligations are discriminatory measures, not neutral risk categories.

groups.name: Religious adaptation and spiritual protection
groups.measures: Prescribe prayers, indulgences and private devotion; restrict crowded observances and visits; substitute home rosaries/alms and reduced church itineraries; hold some observances behind closed doors; relax Lenten food rules; assign segregated confessors and preserve spiritual benefits for outside-church burials.
groups.analysis: Adapts religious obligations to restrictions and supports continuity of religious life. Spiritual practices were meaningful in the historical system; their religious claims are distinct from demonstrated biological effects.

groups.name: Enforcement, integrity and disclosure incentives
groups.measures: Fines, confiscation, corporal punishment, galley service and threatened death; informer rewards; pursuit of escapees and stolen goods; sanctions for forgery, impersonation, false cleansing certificates, bribes and obstruction; repeated amnesties and immunity for timely truthful disclosure.
groups.analysis: Enforces compliance but can also create reasons to hide. Repeated amnesties, restitution and compensation show attempts to counter those incentives; a prescribed penalty is not proof of execution in every case.

groups.name: Selective reopening and adjustment
groups.measures: Suspend, reopen and re-suspend particular places; preserve narrower bans on bedding or nonmetal goods while admitting people and essentials; retain certificates and guards; use health inquiries, last-case dates, elapsed time and cleansing; revoke selected reporting/entry restrictions while maintaining core surveillance; reopen courts with crowd controls.
groups.analysis: A sequence of conditional decisions, not a fixed package. Repeated local decrees are policy changes or renewals and must not be counted as distinct intervention technologies.

chapters.summary: Suspend commerce between Naples and its territory and the whole Papal State after reports of suspected contagious disease.
provisions: Ban entry and commerce involving people, goods and animals from Naples and its territory, including transit and receiving or assisting prohibited arrivals.
Apply death and confiscation penalties to offenders and accomplices, including privileged and ecclesiastical persons; restrict ordinary mitigation for minors.

chapters.title: Health passes, guarded borders and status-based exclusions
chapters.summary: Control arrivals and borders through inspected routes, guarded entries and free individualized health certificates. Require travel/lodging records and prohibit forged or transferred passes and bribery. Impose explicit status-based exclusions on vagabonds, able-bodied beggars, Roma and Jews, even with health papers.
provisions: Require individualized health passes with name, origin and identifying traits, authorized signatures/seals, route endorsements and controlled destinations.
Prohibit blank, transferred or forged passes; issue passes free and prohibit gifts or bribes.
Inspect and register travellers and lodgings; require hosts to report illness, including in their own households.
Repair and seal walls and unauthorized entrances; guard coasts and towers, signal danger by fire/smoke, and restrict nighttime border passage and contact with prohibited vessels or coasts.
Exclude vagabonds, able-bodied beggars, Roma (the original uses 'Zingaro') and Jews even when they hold health passes. This is explicit status discrimination, not a demonstrated infection category.

chapters.title: Street cleaning, waste disposal and roaming pigs
chapters.summary: Order cleaning of streets, courtyards, markets, butcheries, drains, wells and stagnant underground spaces; assign landlord/tenant cleaning costs, regulate waste disposal and prohibit roaming pigs. Several wastes are directed into the flowing Tiber.
provisions: Clean streets, courtyards, markets, butcheries and drains; remove dead animals, manure, stagnant liquids and other filth.
Empty stagnant cellars and wells; fill abandoned wells. Landlords have three days, then tenants must arrange cleaning within three days at the landlord's expense, deductible from rent.
Remove slaughterhouse blood and offal the same day, shell peas/beans indoors, and require daily market cleaning.
The specified disposal destination for several wastes is the flowing Tiber; this should not be described as modern wastewater treatment.
Prohibit roaming pigs; authorize their killing and distribution of carcasses to charitable institutions.

chapters.title: Report illness and deaths; protect exposed property
chapters.summary: Require doctors, clergy and cohabitants to report illness and deaths; appoint district notaries; promise property indemnity and restrict unauthorized burial, goods removal and entry into closed houses.
provisions: Require immediate reporting of all household illness, even without plague signs, and deaths, including onset, circumstances and attending doctor; one household report suffices but clergy retain an independent duty.
Promise reimbursement of disinfection expenses and the assessed value of burned possessions to prompt reporters.

Require signed evening physician lists including previously reported patients; suspected contagion must be reported immediately. Ordinary noncontagious hospital patients have a reporting exception, but hospital staff must report.

Require notification of changes of address and truthful replies during household inspections; inns need permission to admit people already ill and must report guests becoming ill.
Prohibit changes of name or aliases and attempts to bypass gates or walls, including by river, with persons, letters or goods.
Reward informers with a third of confiscations; extend penalties across status groups and specify expiry of this emergency regulation when health gate guards are removed.

Prescribe particular cleanliness rules for the ghetto.

Investigate health offenders, suspects and their contacts, especially escapees from sealed houses or lazarettos.

supplements.title: Narrative and administration
supplements.summary: Central and district organization, controlled supply channels, relief funding, medical deployment and the progression from initial containment to later reopening. This section often describes measures whose legal texts recur in chapters 42–245.
supplements.note: Use to understand sequence and institutions; not additional independent NPIs each time the narrative repeats an order.

supplements.title: Infant feeding and segregated care
supplements.summary: Recruit wet nurses for affected infants and use goats/goat milk where nursing provision fails; organize separate Jewish medical and burial arrangements and external community support.
supplements.note: Reported historical arrangements; infant feeding is a care/support intervention, not a plague cure.

supplements.title: Relief and financing
supplements.summary: Combine public funds and charity, including national community arrangements and separate facilities for Spanish and Portuguese beneficiaries.
supplements.note: Supports the relief/financing group; not all support was supplied on identical terms.

supplements.title: Physical facilities and separation
supplements.summary: Plans of gates, cordons, hospitals, quarantine and cleansing facilities and burial grounds; barriers and separated flows; controlled food, wine, money, mail and goods transfer.
supplements.note: Infrastructure implements several policy groups and should not be counted as twenty-seven unrelated intervention types.

supplements.title: Sanitation, food and occupational separation
supplements.summary: Discuss healthy siting, foul material in roads, food and water, and established passport, gate and cleansing practices; cite separation of exposed physicians and infected institutional residents.
supplements.note: Some examples are from other times or jurisdictions. Theory itself is not an implemented Roman intervention.

supplements.title: Recognition and decision thresholds
supplements.summary: Convene physicians promptly and weigh the safer opinion if they disagree; do not require mass deaths to recognize plague. Yet avoid immediately interrupting commerce or alarming citizens before evident contagion passes between houses.
supplements.note: A nuanced recommendation balancing detection and disruption; not a blanket instruction to close everything at first suspicion.

supplements.title: Early warning and crop protection
supplements.summary: Interpret weather, crops and animal events as possible warnings; report paid workers burning and deeply burying destructive locust swarms before the epidemic.
supplements.note: Agricultural pest destruction is not evidence of plague-directed flea or rodent control. Prognostic beliefs are not reliable modern diagnostics.

supplements.title: Air, sanitation, burial and rulers
supplements.summary: Remove filth and stagnant water, maintain drains and aqueducts, limit retting and foul industries, bury promptly and deeply outside towns, choose dry/elevated residences and protect rulers. Also recommend tree belts, aromatic or sulfur/gunpowder fires, vinegar, wind-dependent windows, bells and cannon to disperse supposed corrupted air.
supplements.note: Combines sanitation with miasmatic reasoning. Presence in this chapter does not establish implementation in Rome.

supplements.title: Moral and religious protection
supplements.summary: Prayer, penance and divine assistance; moral purification and punishment of wrongdoing; limit exposed gallows corpses and crowded executions.
supplements.note: Religious and moral claims belong to the historical explanatory system, not demonstrated infection mechanisms.

supplements.title: Food security and water protection
supplements.summary: Count grain against population needs; restrict exports, hoarding, monopoly and diversion; compel fair-price sale; audit grain funds; finance imports and relief and, if needed, tax privileged groups. Inspect food and prevent adulteration. Protect aqueducts/cisterns and prohibit dumping, dirty laundry and bathing in public water.
supplements.note: Food/water governance is broader than contact restriction; these are recommendations, not all independently verified Roman enactments.

supplements.title: Institutions and transmission barriers
supplements.summary: Handle and fumigate mail with tools; inspect ships and cargo; guard gates and rivers; quarantine suspect arrivals and cleanse goods outside the city; provide water, drainage and separated staff/patients. Recommend forty-day stations and two successive quarantines for convalescents; preserve essential food markets and supply confined households.
supplements.note: Do not project these suggested durations onto every earlier Roman order. Historical leper/convent examples and claimed chemical air tests are contextual doctrine.

supplements.title: Personal regimen and occupational precautions
supplements.summary: Moderate food, exercise, sleep and emotions; boil impure water; use clean smooth/waxed clothing, vinegar washing and mouth/nose cloths; avoid patient breath and downwind exposure.
supplements.note: Historical prophylaxis: listing a measure is not an endorsement of its efficacy.

supplements.title: Clinical and ritual adjuncts
supplements.summary: Discuss amulets, pharmaceutical and surgical remedies and reported treatment experience; reject arsenic/mercury amulets as dangerous while accepting other amulets, acknowledge no dependable specific antidote, and question some harmful conventional treatment.
supplements.note: Drugs and clinical procedures are outside the nonpharmaceutical public-health inventory. No therapeutic recipe is reproduced.

supplements.title: Explanatory theories and historical allegations
supplements.summary: Definitions, susceptibility, air and weather, astrological theories, internal putrefaction, alleged poisoning/demonic causation, disease taxonomy and prognosis. Chapter 252 includes historical antisemitic accusations and extraordinary corpse stories, with skepticism about many such accounts.
supplements.note: These claims are not verified causes or Roman health instructions. Count concrete precautions under their functional group; do not count each causal theory as an intervention.

glossary.definition: An institution used to isolate, observe or care for people and to manage suspect goods. Gastaldi describes distinct facilities and staff roles; the term does not always mean the same patient category.
A period or arrangement of separation for people or belongings regarded as exposed or suspect. Durations vary in the Roman documents; forty days is not a universal rule across this collection.
In this catalogue, separation of sick or potentially infectious people. This modern analytical label does not imply that seventeenth-century authorities used today's diagnostic definitions.
An official document stating identity, origin, route or permitted movement. Some orders require endorsements at checkpoints; a certificate did not override every territorial or status-based ban.
Guarded boundaries intended to prevent unauthorized entry, exit or exchange around places considered infected or suspect.
Historical administrative classifications for people, teams, goods or places considered free from, or exposed to, contagion. They are not laboratory findings or judgments about personal worth.

The historical treatment of possessions or premises using procedures such as washing, boiling, airing, fumigation and selective burning. The label does not certify that a procedure sterilized an object.
Treatment with fumes or smoke, applied to rooms, belongings and other materials under historical contagion and air theories. Its inclusion records practice, not a modern recommendation.
A district of Rome. The programme assigned reporting, inspection and care responsibilities through district officials and notaries.
The central health congregation directing the papal response, supported by commissioners and local officials.
The health notice placed on a sealed house. Removing it, moving it to an unaffected house or impersonating health officials was explicitly prohibited.
A time-limited offer of immunity for truthful disclosure or surrender of suspect property, with specified conditions and exclusions. Repeated amnesties did not erase all health offences.

Rome's compulsory Jewish residential district, subjected to separate medical, reporting, supply and burial administration. The catalogue distinguishes relief from discriminatory confinement and exclusions.

Nonpharmaceutical intervention: an analytical term for measures such as surveillance, separation, movement restrictions and environmental controls. It is not Gastaldi's terminology, and a chapter or decree is not one unique NPI.
An order establishes what authorities required. Its text alone does not prove compliance, uniform enforcement or effectiveness; those questions need additional records and analysis.
